text: The festival I'd like to describe is the Mid-Autumn Festival, which takes place in September or October, on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month. It's often called the Children's Festival, because it's a special time for kids. In the weeks before, the streets fill up with colourful lanterns, masks and stalls selling mooncakes. On the night itself, families gather to share a meal, eat mooncakes and enjoy fruit like pomelos and persimmons. Children carry paper lanterns and join lion dances in the neighbourhood, while adults sit outside and admire the full moon. I remember as a child waiting all day for the evening, because my father always helped me make a lantern in the shape of a star. What I like most about the festival is the warm, relaxed mood. It's not as hectic as the Lunar New Year, but it brings people together just the same. In my view, it's important because it reminds us to value family and to care about children. It also keeps old traditions alive, such as lantern making and lion dancing, which might otherwise be forgotten as life becomes more modern. Nowadays, many people give mooncakes to colleagues and friends as gifts, and some worry the festival is becoming too commercial. Still, whenever I look up at the bright moon with my family, I feel that the spirit of the festival is very much alive.

text: The bicycle looks simple, but it took nearly a century to reach its modern form. The first ancestor was built in Germany in 1817 by Karl von Drais. His 'running machine' had two wheels and a wooden frame, but no pedals; riders pushed along the ground with their feet. It was popular for a short time, but poor roads and some accidents meant that many towns banned it. In the 1860s, French makers added pedals to the front wheel. These machines were uncomfortable on rough streets, so people called them 'boneshakers'. Later models had a huge front wheel, because a larger wheel meant a greater distance with each turn of the pedals. These 'penny-farthings' were fast, but also dangerous: a rider who hit a stone could be thrown over the handlebars. The big change came in the 1880s with the 'safety bicycle'. It had two wheels of equal size, a chain connecting the pedals to the back wheel, and a lower seat. Soon afterwards, inflatable rubber tyres made the ride much smoother. Bicycles became cheap enough for ordinary workers to buy, and they gave people a new kind of freedom. Women in particular found that cycling allowed them to travel alone, and some historians believe it helped change attitudes to women's clothing and independence. During the twentieth century, cars became the main form of transport in many countries, and cycling became less common. However, in the last twenty years, bikes have returned to city streets. Governments build cycle lanes to reduce traffic and pollution, and many cities offer bikes for rent through mobile phone apps. Electric bicycles, which have a small motor to help the rider, are especially popular because they make hills and long journeys easier. Cycling is also healthy, because regular exercise strengthens the heart and reduces stress. The Netherlands has a particularly strong cycling culture, and there are more bicycles there than people.
